title: Superposition
text:
Swerdlow’s Fig. 1.2 does not show one model. It shows two — the eccentric and the epicyclic form of Ptolemy’s solar model — in one plane. That is a superposition:
Every name of a member gets the member’s prefix (Ecc.S, Epi.S'); the names the text identifies become one (O, lamA, kappa_bar). Identification says that the two models are about the same earth, the same apsidal direction, the same mean motion. It adds no geometry. Only inputs — parameters of one unit, kinematic variables — and the observer can be identified; a text that identifies two constructed points is refused:
The superposition is again a model: pure geometry over the parameters of both members. In it the two suns are two points. They coincide for some parameter values and not for others; nothing in the superposition says which.

title: Representation, model, description
text: Three things are easily run together: the model, the texts and pictures that represent it, and the prose that describes and uses it.

title: Representation, model, description
text:
The model
The model is not a text. It is the geometry: the function from parameter values and states to configurations, with what holds of it. Ptolemy’s eccentric solar model is the same model whether Ptolemy, Regiomontanus, Swerdlow or an astra text states it. That is why an astra model text carries three different names: whose model it is (attributed "Ptolemy"), the text whose use of the model is analysed (witness fr:kepler-sec/Swerdlow2026/…), and who wrote the description (author "Gerd Graßhoff"). Swerdlow uses and explains the model; he is not its author, and neither is the author of the astra text.

title: Representation, model, description
text:
Representations
A representation is anything that determines the model: Ptolemy’s prose and figure; Swerdlow’s prose and his figures; the astra model text; the compiled list of operations; the sheet. Two representations represent the same model when they agree in every configuration — what diff tests as the same geometry up to renaming.
A figure represents less and more than the model: less, because it shows one state under one set of values; more, because it chooses a view and often other values than the attested ones. Swerdlow’s Fig. 1.4 and his Fig. 1.2 draw the same eccentric model in two states, two orientations and with an exaggerated eccentricity. In astra/1 they are two figure texts of one model.

title: Representation, model, description
section: What a diagram of two models is

title: Representation, model, description
text:
Equivalence is not identity
The eccentric and the epicyclic form are different models. Under hypotheses they are equivalent in what is compared — the position of the sun, or only its direction — and they stay different in everything else: in the one the sun moves uniformly on a circle about E, in the other its motion is compounded of two. Swerdlow notes that only Kepler drew a consequence from that difference (p. 20).

title: Deep reading
text:
A deep reading takes a few pages of a source and checks every assertion on them: the quotation is verified against the transcription, every number is recomputed, every geometrical statement is a proposition of a model or a step of a derivation, and every result comes with its evidence — the crop of the page. The record is a YAML file (readings/<name>.yaml), the report is reproducible (famulus-astra reading readings/<name>.yaml), and every item points back to its paragraph.
An item:
formal is sexagesimal arithmetic or one of
check_of distinguishes the author’s own statements (print) from historical figures the author reports (reported): a discrepancy in the first is about the page, in the second about the source reported. A quotation that is not in the paragraph’s transcription fails the run.

The two discrepancies of the print are misprints: the sign rule for the equation of centre names the same condition in both clauses, and the advance of al-Battānī’s apogee is given as 16;37° where the two longitudes on the page differ by 16;47°.
The seven discrepancies in reported figures are facts about the sources, not about Swerdlow’s page. Two are Ptolemy’s roundings of his mean motions. One is al-Battānī’s maximum equation as Regiomontanus transmits it, 1;59,10° against 1;59,9° from his eccentricity. Four belong to the determination of the parameters from the seasons: inverted exactly, the model gives e = 2;29,28 and λ_A = 65;35° from the two reported arcs, and e = 2;28,58 and λ_A = 65;26° from the day counts. Ptolemy’s 2;29,30 and 65;30° follow from his rounded arcs within the rounding of a chord computation, not from the day counts. The paragraph itself calls the derivation sensitive to errors in the intervals.

title: Outputs
section: A line of sight and a narrated figure
text:
A line of sight and a narrated figure
A figure can draw the line of sight from an observer to a body, in a colour of its own, and it can be narrated: shown and described stage by stage.
label sight line(O, Ecc.S)
stage eccentric "The eccentric form: the sun S moves uniformly about E." show Ecc
stage epicyclic "The epicyclic form: the sun S' is carried on the epicycle." show Epi
stage both      "Both forms in one figure." show Ecc, Epi
stage sight     "The line of sight from O to the sun: one line for both forms." reveal sight
stage run       "Through a whole revolution the two suns stay together." play
A stage shows members of a superposition (show; none named: all), lets labels of a kind appear and stay (reveal), stands at a state (at kappa_bar = 90°) or runs through one revolution (play), and says one sentence. The page shows that sentence under the figure; the stages are stepped through one by one or played in turn, and a change of stage fades. A narrated figure opens at its first stage and does not run by itself. In print the still is followed by the sentences as a numbered list. famulus-astra svg <figure> --stage <name> draws the still of one stage.
The narration is checked with the figure: a stage that names an unknown member, reveals a kind the figure does not label, repeats a name or stands at a state of another variable makes the figure not well-formed.
A project can hold astra texts of its own beside the shared ones: famulus-astra --root <folder> … (repeatable), or the folders named in FAMULUS_ASTRA_PATH. A Famulus notebook does this for <project>/astra.

This page is the language reference. It is rendered from spec/astra-1.md, the normative text; the op-set with its exact semantics follows from spec/ops.yaml, the rules of derivation from spec/rules.yaml (Derivations).
Status: active, revisable (10 Nov 2026; replaces the draft of 9 Nov, which wrote geometry, values and depicted state into one text). Normative for famulus-astronomica. The op-set is ops.yaml, the rules of derivation are rules.yaml, the test vectors ops-vectors.json and model-vectors.json.

title: The language astra/1
text:
1. What is told apart
A historical astronomical model is a geometrical construction with a kinematic variable. Four things are easily run together and are kept apart here, each in a text of its own kind:









what it is
kind of text




the model
the pure geometry: parameter symbols, kinematic variables, the construction, the observables. It holds for every admissible parameter value and every state. It has no values.
model


a parametrisation
values for the parameters of one model, each with its source or a stated gap, and whose values they are. One model has many.
parametrisation


a state
a value of the kinematic variable (or a time, through the variable’s law). Not a text: an argument, at kappa_bar = 41°.
—


a configuration
a model under a parametrisation in a state: every object has coordinates. Computed, never written.
—



Two more things are done with models, and a fifth kind of text shows them:









what it is
kind of text




a superposition
several models in one plane, with their inputs identified (one earth, one apsidal direction, one mean anomaly). It adds no geometry and states nothing across its members. It is again a model.
superposition


a derivation
geometrical reasoning in a model or a superposition: hypotheses, auxiliary constructions, propositions derived from named premises by named rules, quantities computed or determined, a conclusion.
derivation


a figure
a depiction: what it draws, with which values, in which state, with which labels and view.
figure



Three roles of persons and texts are kept apart in every text: attributed (whose model, whose values), witness (the text whose use of the model is analysed, by fr: address) and author (who wrote this astra text). The author of a text about Ptolemy’s model that follows Swerdlow’s exposition is neither Ptolemy nor Swerdlow.

title: The language astra/1
text:
2. Lexical form

UTF-8, one statement per line. A ; surrounded by whitespace separates statements on one line; a ; between digits is sexagesimal (2;30). # starts a comment. One text per file; the first statement names its kind.
Identifiers [A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_']*, dotted for the member of a superposition (Ecc.S). Text ids may contain hyphens and dots (solar-eccentric.ptolemy). The printed symbol of a name is given by display <name> "<text>"; one underscore in it marks a subscript (λ_A).
Numbers: decimal 12.5 or sexagesimal <int>;<p1>,<p2>,… (2;30 = 2.5, 365;14,48). A trailing ° makes an angle. The written form is kept.
Strings in double quotes. fr: addresses are a token of their own.

title: The language astra/1

3. Model

A model text that gives a parameter a value, or a source to a value, is refused. A range may depend on earlier parameters (in (0, R / 2)). A kinematic variable without a law is free: its states are not ordered in time. Time enters only through a law. Every name is defined before it is used; nothing is placed by coordinates except the observer, the origin.
Types: number, angle, length, time, rate, point, vector, line, circle, ellipse. Arithmetic + − * / with units (angle ± angle, length · number, length / length → number, length · length as an intermediate, point ± vector → point, point − point → vector).

text:
4. Parametrisation
parametrisation <id> of <model or superposition> "<title>"
attributed "<whose values>"     witness fr:…     author "…"
<param> = <expr> ["note"] (source fr:… | gap "<why>")

A value may be an expression in parameters that already have a value (Epi.r = Ecc.e). A parametrisation is complete when every parameter has a value, admissible when every value lies in its range, attested when every value has a source or a stated gap. A partial parametrisation is legitimate and reported as such; what needs the missing values cannot be computed with it, and says so.

Every name of a member is prefixed; identified names become one. Only parameters of one unit, kinematic variables and the observer can be identified. That two constructed points coincide is a proposition, to be derived under hypotheses; a superposition that tried to identify them is refused.

text:

with <parametrisation>

at <variable> = <angle>                  the depicted state   (or: at t = <days> d)
up <angle>      fit [a, b, …]      speed <n> s
label angle <angle> at <V> from <arm> to <arm> [arrow]       arm: a point, an angle name, or `aries` (0°)

label arrow <P> on <circle>      label segment line(P, Q)      label dashed line(P, Q)

label direction <angle> from <P> [dashed]      label zodiac at <O> on <circle> [full]

stage <name> "<sentence>" [show <member>, …] [reveal <label kind>, …] [at <variable> = <angle> | play]
Narration (1.1, 11 Nov 2026). The stage statements of a figure, in their order, are its narration: a figure that is shown and described step by step. A stage

shows members of a superposition (show Ecc; none named: all of them) — what belongs to another member is not drawn; what belongs to no member (the observer, a line of sight) always is;
reveals labels by their kind (reveal sight): a kind that some stage reveals is not drawn before that stage and stays from it on;
stands at a state (at kappa_bar = 90°; none given: the state it is entered in) or runs through a revolution (play);
says one sentence, which the page shows under the figure and the print sets beside the still of the stage.

A figure without stages is drawn and moves as before. The narration is checked with the figure: an unknown member, a kind the figure does not label, a name used twice or a state of another variable makes the figure not well-formed; a kind that no stage ever reveals, or one the figure does not draw, makes it not labelled. The page opens at the first stage and does not run by itself; the transport steps through the stages or plays them all.
Texts of a project. A workspace reads the shared texts (examples/) and, beside them, the folders named by --root <dir> (repeatable) or FAMULUS_ASTRA_PATH: the own texts of a project, e.g. a notebook’s figures. An id used in two folders is an error.
A figure of a derivation draws the derivation’s context, auxiliary constructions included, and can show one step at a time: the points and segments the step speaks of.

title: The language astra/1
text:
7. Derivation
derivation <id> in <model or superposition> "<title>"
given <h>: equal(<param>, <expr>) ["meaning"]            a hypothesis: it restricts the parameter space
construct <name> = <expr> ["meaning"]                     an auxiliary construction
derive <d>: <predicate>(…) from <premises> by <rule> ["meaning"]
show <A>: <predicate>(…) ["claim"]                          a sub-argument: the claim, then its steps (indented), then
  …                                                         qed from <steps> [by <rule>]
cases ["by what"]                                          inside a `show`: the claim is argued case by case
  case <n>: when <condition>(…)[, <condition>(…)] ["…"]     … qed from <steps>;   the `show` closes with `qed by cases`
suppose <n>: <condition>(…) ["…"]                           restricts the steps that follow, to the end of the block
conclude <predicate>(…) from <premises> [by <rule>]       the conclusion (a further `conclude` needs its rule)
conclude equivalent(<P>, <Q>, position | direction) from <premises>
compute <x> = <expr> | max(<expr>) [at <variable> = <angle>] with <parametrisation> [reported <value> source fr:…]
determine [<name>:] <p>, <q> from <obs>: <a> -> <b> = <n> d | <arc>°, … with <parametrisation> [reported <p> = <v>, … source fr:…]
Premises: a given or an earlier step by name, def <object> (the construction of an object), prop <name> (a proposition stated in the model). Rules (rules.yaml): Elements <book>.<n>, lemma <name>, trigonometry <name>, common notion 1, common notion 5, construction, algebra, expansion, cases. A case name or a supposition name is a premise as well: it cites the condition.
Predicates of a step: those of a model (parallel, perpendicular, coincident, collinear, on, equal) and less(a, b) — strictly, in every configuration; where equality occurs in isolated states these are reported — and approximately(a, b, small: <ratio>, order: <n>): the two sides agree to order n in the small ratio. It is tested at the ratios 10⁻², 10⁻³, 10⁻⁴: the relative difference must fall like the n-th power.
Conditions (of cases, suppositions and rules): collinear, noncollinear, distinct, same_direction, same_side, opposite_side, between, right_angle.
Blocks. The inside of a closed show cannot be cited from outside it; the show itself can. The steps of a case are checked only in the configurations that satisfy its condition, the steps after a suppose only where the supposition holds. qed by cases requires that every case reaches the claim and that the conditions together cover every sampled configuration; an uncovered state is named in the report.
equivalent(P, Q, position) is the proposition that the bodies of the members P and Q coincide; equivalent(P, Q, direction) that they are seen from the observer in one direction. Equivalence is a relation between two models, relative to the givens and to what is compared; it is a conclusion, never an assumption.
Four questions, each presupposing the previous:

grounded — every premise resolves to a given, an earlier step, a construction or a stated proposition.
true — every proposition holds in all sampled configurations that satisfy the givens. A term undefined in isolated states (an angle at a vanished triangle) makes those states undefined, not the step false.
justified — every step is licensed by its rule, in one of these grades:

rule: an instance of a proposition, lemma or definition: the rule’s variables bind to points so that a conclusion of the rule is the step’s proposition (up to the symmetries of the predicates), each hypothesis of the rule is a cited premise, and the rule’s configuration conditions hold. States in which they fail are the degenerate states of the step; more than a few isolated ones and the step is not justified;
equality: the two sides are joined by the cited equalities (Common Notion 1);
construction: read off the cited constructions — the proposition speaks only of the cited objects and what they are built from, and holds over the whole parameter space without the givens;
calculation: an equality or inequality from cited ones; confirmed numerically, the calculation is not replayed;
approximation (rule expansion): the stated order is confirmed at three sizes of the small ratio;
cases: every case reaches the claim and the cases cover every configuration; a show is justified when the steps it closes with are its claim. A step that is true but none of these is true, not justified: a gap in the reasoning.

conclusive — the conclusion is reached from the givens. For every given the parameter space is sampled with that given lifted: a proposition that then fails needs the given; if the given is not cited on the way to it, it is a tacit premise. Givens the conclusion does not need and steps not on the way to it are noted.

compute evaluates a quantity under a parametrisation (a maximum over the states, or at a state) and compares it with a reported value at the precision in which that value is written. determine solves parameters from observed intervals — the time, or the arc of mean motion, in which an observable goes from one value to another — by inverting the model numerically, reports whether the solution is the only one, and compares.
A derivation that passes is reasoning whose every proposition is true in the model and whose every step names a rule that licenses it. It is not a formal proof in an axiomatic system: truth is tested on samples, rules are matched as schemas, configuration conditions are evaluated numerically.

The argument document (astra-argument/1)
famulus-astra argument <derivation> [--format json|md|typst|html] writes a derivation as an argument for reading: head, the model (every object with construction and meaning), hypotheses H1…, constructions, the argument as a tree — each node with a hierarchical number, kind (sub-argument, case, step, supposition, conclusion), the claim in prose, the proposition in the notation of the figure, premises as references, the rule with wording and locus, status and mark (✓ rule instance, ◦ read off the construction, ≈ calculation or expansion, ? true but not justified, ✗ false, · supposed), the binding, conditions and degenerate states — the conclusion, what the checks say, and the figure. Three depths: overview, steps, full. The web component <astra-argument> (web/astra-argument/) renders the document with collapse and expand.


7a. The exposition document (astra-exposition/1)
An exposition sets a derivation beside the source it reconstructs. It is not a sixth kind of astra text: it is a YAML file under expositions/ that names a derivation and divides a segment of a source into passages.

9. Evaluation

Python (evaluate.py) and JavaScript (astra-runtime.js) implement it and replay the same vectors. A parameter without value is an error as soon as anything but a range or a law needs it; a state that fixes no variable is an error.

10. Reference objects
fr:astra/<id> is a text of any kind; fr:astra/<id>/<object> a parameter, variable, constructed object, observable or proposition of a context, a value of a parametrisation, a given, step, computation or the conclusion of a derivation. Views ~sheet ~source ~check, for figures ~svg ~animation. The grammar is in famulus-ref/2 (reserved_namespaces.astra, 2.4.0); the resolver names the kind of text.

title: The language astra/1
section: 10a. The package and the texts of a project
text:
10a. The package and the texts of a project
The shared texts are offered as a package: PACKAGE.yaml (schema famulus-package/1, written by famulus-astra package --write, never by hand) lists every text with its kind, its group (the folder under examples/: solar, kepler, euler), the SHA-256 of its source and the ids of the texts it names (needs: the model of a parametrisation, the members of a superposition, the context and the values of a figure or a derivation). Expositions are listed with the kind exposition in the group of the derivation they rest on. famulus-astra package --check says where the manifest and the texts differ; the test suite fails when it is behind. fr:astra names the package (version, digest, groups); fr:astra/<group> lists a group.
A document that uses astra declares what it imports: the package (fr:astra), a group (fr:astra/solar) or one text (fr:astra/solar-eccentric), optionally pinned with @rel:<version>. A text comes with the texts it rests on (its closure over needs). Exactly the imported texts and the document’s own texts are available to it; the importing system decides what a use outside that is (a Famulus notebook project reports it as a gap). The hashes let the importing system record against which state of a text it was written, and say when that state changed.
A project’s own texts stand in a folder of its own (--root <dir>, repeatable, or FAMULUS_ASTRA_PATH) and may be of every kind: a model, a parametrisation, a superposition of an own model with a shared one, a figure, a derivation. They name shared texts by id; a shared text never names a project’s text, and a project’s text never enters the manifest. An id used both in the package and in a project is an error of that id.
famulus-astra positions <figure> [<point> …] [--steps n] [--with <parametrisation>] [--json] lists where named points stand at equally spaced states of one revolution, and for two points their distance with its maximum. It states what was computed with which values; that two points coincide for every admissible value is what a derivation shows.

title: The language astra/1
text:
11. Representation, model, description
The model is not a text. It is the geometry — the function from parameter values and states to configurations, with what holds of it. The astra model text, a printed figure, Ptolemy’s or Swerdlow’s prose, the op list, a sheet, an animation are representations of it; two representations of one model agree in every configuration (diff: the same geometry up to renaming). A parametrised model is still not a picture: a figure adds a state and a view, and often other values than the attested ones.
Equivalence relates two models, not two representations: under stated hypotheses they agree in what is compared (the position of the body, or only its direction) and differ in everything else. A superposition is the scene in which such a relation can be stated, and a derivation is what establishes it.
A describing text refers to the model through names — “complete parallelogram OESC”. The astra texts make those names resolvable, so that prose, figure and derivation speak of the same objects, and so that what the prose asserts can be checked: as a proposition of the model, a step of a derivation, or a computed quantity.

title: Famulus Astronomica
text:
A historical astronomical model is a geometrical construction with a kinematic variable: a few lengths and angles, one or two circles, a point that moves, and an observer who measures directions. Texts about such models do four different things at once: they describe a geometry, give it numbers, show it in one position, and reason about it. astra/1 writes each of the four as plain text of its own kind.
The first texts describe Ptolemy’s solar model in its eccentric and its epicyclic form, as Noel Swerdlow sets it out in The Renaissance of Astronomy (2026), chapter 1. The model is Ptolemy’s; the text whose use of the model is analysed is Swerdlow’s; the astra texts are by Gerd Graßhoff. Every astra text says all three (attributed, witness, author).

title: Famulus Astronomica
text:
Sixty seconds
model solar-eccentric "Ptolemy's solar model, eccentric form"
attributed "Ptolemy"
witness fr:kepler-sec/Swerdlow2026/0049/p04 "the construction, p. 19"
author "Gerd Graßhoff"
frame geocentric
param R    : length "radius of the eccentric"         in (1, 1000)
param e    : length "eccentricity, the distance OE"   in (0, R / 2)
param lamA : angle  "longitude of the apogee"
variable kappa_bar : angle "mean anomaly about E, counted from the apogee"
O   = observer                        "earth"
E   = O + polar(e, lamA)              "centre of the eccentric"
ecc = circle(E, R)                    "the eccentric"
S   = E + polar(R, lamA + kappa_bar)  "sun"
body sun at S
observe lam = direction(O, S)         "true longitude"
No number stands in it. The numbers are a second text, and there can be several:
parametrisation solar-eccentric.ptolemy of solar-eccentric "Ptolemy's values"
attributed "Ptolemy"
R    = 60        source fr:kepler-sec/Swerdlow2026/0052/p05
e    = 2;30      source fr:kepler-sec/Swerdlow2026/0052/p05
lamA = 65;30°    source fr:kepler-sec/Swerdlow2026/0052/p05
A state is a value of the kinematic variable, kappa_bar = 41°. Model, values and state together give a configuration; a figure draws one, an animation runs through them.
Reasoning comes after the construction, as an operation of its own:
derivation solar-equivalence-equal-radii in solar-eccentric-epicyclic "…"
given h1: equal(Epi.R', Ecc.R)
given h2: equal(Epi.r, Ecc.e)
derive d2: parallel(line(Ecc.E, Ecc.S), line(O, Epi.C)) from d1 by Elements I.28

…

First whether the two are the same geometry up to renaming — a structural signature: every object as its expression with the names replaced by their kinds — then what one construction has that the other lacks.

solar-eccentric ↔ solar-epicyclic: different geometries
  parameters
    − R
    − e
    + R'
    + r
  construction
    − E (point) = O + polar(e, lamA)

    + def (circle) = circle(O, R')
    + C (point) = O + polar(R', lamA + kappa_bar)

The page says: “To construct the epicyclic model, complete parallelogram OESC”. It names the figure in which the reasoning can be seen. The reasoning itself, step by step, with the proposition that licenses each step:
# The equivalence of the two forms when the radii are equal: the reasoning that Swerdlow's Fig. 1.2 exhibits.
# The page (p. 19, scan page 49, paragraph 3): "To construct the epicyclic model, complete parallelogram OESC and
# let C be the center of an epicycle of radius r = e moving uniformly through κ̄ on a concentric circle about O of
# radius R' = R while the sun S moves in the opposite direction through κ̄ about C from OC extended to the apogee
# of the epicycle, so that r is always parallel to the apsidal line AB."

# which there is no parallelogram — the sun at the apogee and at the perigee — are set out here.

title: Derivations
text:
Four questions
Grounded. Every premise resolves: to a given, an earlier step, the construction of an object (def Ecc.S), or a proposition stated in the model (prop p1).
True. Every proposition holds in all sampled configurations that satisfy the givens.
Justified. Every step is licensed by its rule, in one of four grades.

An instance of a rule. For d6 … by Elements I.33 the matcher binds the proposition’s variables, A = O, B = C, C = E, D = S, so that I.33’s conclusion is the step’s proposition, finds its two hypotheses among the cited premises (d2 and d5), and evaluates its configuration conditions.
Common Notion 1. The two sides of an equality are joined by the cited equalities.
Read off the construction. The proposition speaks only of the cited objects and what they are built from, and holds over the whole parameter space without the givens. ES = R is read off the construction of S.
Calculation. An equality from cited equalities, confirmed numerically; the calculation is not replayed.

Conclusive. For every given, the parameter space is sampled with that given lifted. A proposition that then fails needs the given. If the given is not cited on the way to it, it is a tacit premise.

title: Derivations
section: What the figure supplies: configuration conditions and degenerate states
text:
What the figure supplies: configuration conditions and degenerate states
Euclid’s propositions take something from the figure: that points are distinct, that two points lie on the same side of a line, that two segments point the same way. In the rule table these are configuration conditions, and they are evaluated in every sampled configuration. I.33 needs A, B, C not to lie on one line. At κ̄ = 0° and κ̄ = 180° the parallelogram OESC collapses into the apsidal line, and I.33 does not apply. These are the degenerate states of the step. The conclusion is true there as well, but the parallelogram does not reach it, and the printed figure, drawn at κ̄ ≈ 41°, does not show that.

title: Derivations
text:
Sub-arguments and cases
The derivation above therefore argues its claim — the two suns are one point — in three cases: off the apsidal line by the parallelogram; at the apogee and at the perigee by adding and subtracting lengths along the line. A case has a condition (when noncollinear(O, Ecc.E, Ecc.S)); its steps are checked only in the configurations that satisfy it; qed by cases requires that the cases together cover every configuration and that each reaches the claim. A sub-argument (show … qed) states a claim and then the steps for it; its inside cannot be cited from outside, which is what makes an overview possible. A supposition (suppose quadrant: right_angle(D, C, E)) restricts the steps after it to one position, as Kepler’s “et sit jam DCE rectus” does. Read as an argument with collapse and expand: Arguments.

If a straight line set up on a straight line make angles, it will make either two right angles or angles equal to two right angles.

Elements I.28
proposition
If a straight line falling on two straight lines make the exterior angle equal to the interior and opposite angle on the same side, or the interior angles on the same side equal to two right angles, the straight lines will be parallel to one another. (case: exterior angle equal to the interior and opposite angle on the same side)
equal(angle(T1, V1, P), angle(T2, V2, Q)) → parallel(line(V1, P), line(V2, Q))

Elements I.29
proposition
A straight line falling on parallel straight lines makes the alternate angles equal to one another, the exterior angle equal to the interior and opposite angle, and the interior angles on the same side equal to two right angles. (case: alternate angles)
parallel(line(P, Q), line(R, S)) → equal(angle(P, Q, R), angle(Q, R, S))
distinct(Q, R); opposite_side(P, S, Q, R)
Heath, vol. I, p. 311


Elements I.30
proposition
Straight lines parallel to the same straight line are also parallel to one another.
parallel(line(A, B), line(M, N)); parallel(line(C, D), line(M, N)) → parallel(line(A, B), line(C, D))
—
Heath, vol. I, p. 314


Elements I.32
proposition
In any triangle, if one of the sides be produced, the exterior angle is equal to the two interior and opposite angles, and the three interior angles of the triangle are equal to two right angles. (case: the exterior angle)
— → equal(angle(A, C, D), angle(C, A, B) + angle(A, B, C))
noncollinear(A, B, C); collinear(B, C, D); between(C, B, D)

Elements I.33
proposition
The straight lines joining equal and parallel straight lines (at the extremities which are) in the same directions (respectively) are themselves also equal and parallel.
parallel(line(A, B), line(C, D)); equal(distance(A, B), distance(C, D)) → parallel(line(A, C), line(B, D)); equal(distance(A, C), distance(B, D))

Elements I.34
proposition
In parallelogrammic areas the opposite sides and angles are equal to one another, and the diameter bisects the areas. (case: opposite sides equal)
parallel(line(A, B), line(C, D)); parallel(line(A, C), line(B, D)) → equal(distance(A, B), distance(C, D)); equal(distance(A, C), distance(B, D))
noncollinear(A, B, C)

Elements I.47
proposition
In right-angled triangles the square on the side subtending the right angle is equal to the squares on the sides containing the right angle.
perpendicular(line(X, F), line(Y, Z)) → equal(distance(X, Y) * distance(X, Y), distance(X, F) * distance(X, F) + distance(Y, F) * distance(Y, F))
collinear(Y, Z, F); distinct(Y, F); distinct(X, F)

proposition
If two triangles have one angle equal to one angle and the sides about the equal angles proportional, the triangles will be equiangular and will have those angles equal which the corresponding sides subtend.
equal(angle(B, A, C), angle(E, D, F)); equal(distance(A, B) / distance(A, C), distance(D, E) / distance(D, F)) → equal(angle(A, B, C), angle(D, E, F)); equal(angle(A, C, B), angle(D, F, E))

title: Derivations
section: What a derivation is and is not
text:
What a derivation is and is not
A derivation that passes is reasoning whose every proposition is true in the model and whose every step names a rule that licenses it. It is not a formal proof in an axiomatic system: truth is tested on samples, rules are matched as schemas, configuration conditions are evaluated numerically, and a hypothesis has to fix a parameter.

title: Arguments
text: A derivation is written to be checked. An argument is the same derivation written to be read: the model first, then what is given, then the steps as a numbered outline with sub-arguments and cases indented, the conclusion, and what the checks say. The format is astra-argument/1; one document, four renderings.

Kepler: the equant


The hypothesis H1 (BC = BA) is stated by Kepler and needed by no step. The two inequalities hold in every position; the supposition of the right angle is needed only for the comparison of the two arcs.
# Kepler, Astronomia nova, Part I, ch. 4 (KGW 3, p. 73; kepler-prim/kgw-03, pidx 71, paragraph 4): the argument
# by which the equant model is charged with making the motion of the orb unequal.
# "Eligatur enim E punctum in circulo, quem Planeta corpore peragrat, connectaturque cum CBA : et sit jam DCE
# rectus, ut et ECF. Cum ergo sint anguli hi aequales, constituti nempe aequalibus temporibus, et DCE exterior
# aequet CBE, CEB interiores : ergo parte CEB ablata, residuus CBE vel DBE minor erit quam DCE. itaque FBE
# major quam DCE vel FCE. Sed DE arcus metitur DBE angulum, et EF arcus angulum EBF. minor ergo DE quam EF. et
# transit Planeta per eos aequalibus temporibus."
# Kepler cites no proposition of Euclid. The propositions that license his steps are supplied here.
derivation kepler-equant-unequal-motion in kepler-equant "About the centre of its circle the planet moves unequally: the arc DE is less than the arc EF, and both are passed in equal times"

author "Gerd Graßhoff"

  derive k1: equal(angle(E, C, D), angle(C, E, B) + angle(E, B, C)) by Elements I.32 "DCE is the exterior angle of the triangle CBE, equal to the interior angles CBE and CEB"
  derive k2: less(angle(E, B, C), angle(E, C, D)) from k1 by common notion 5 "the part CEB taken away, the remainder CBE is less than DCE"
  derive k3: equal(angle(E, B, C), angle(D, B, E)) from def C, def D, def E by construction "CBE or DBE: C and D lie from B on one ray"
  derive k4: less(angle(D, B, E), angle(D, C, E)) from k2, k3 by common notion 1
qed from k4

  derive k7: less(angle(E, C, F), angle(E, B, F)) from lag, k5, k6 by algebra

Exit code

title: Design notes
text: Swerdlow’s page 20 explains a figure in prose: “the result of the two motions is that S moves uniformly in the eccentric about E and the direction OS from the earth to the sun, the diagonal of the parallelogram, is the same in both models”. The figure carries the points, the prose carries the relations, the parameters are elsewhere on page 22, and the motion that makes the figure a model — κ̄ growing uniformly with time — is in the reader’s head. A representational language writes these down, each as what it is: the construction as a model, the numbers as a parametrisation with sources, the relation between two models as a derivation in their superposition. From those texts the figure, the animation, the sheets and the check of every step are derived, not drawn by hand.

title: Design notes
section: What was learned from the geometry packages
text:
What was learned from the geometry packages

GCLC (Janičić) treats a construction as a procedure, not a picture: point, circle k O A, intersec, towards, rotate; free and constructed points are distinct; prove {…} checks a statement over the construction; animation_frames parametrises. astra/1 keeps the procedure view — every object is defined before it is used, so the construction is a directed acyclic graph by construction. GCLC’s prover takes a conjecture and returns a proof; an astra derivation takes the steps a text gives and asks of each whether it is true and whether the rule it names licenses it. It drops coordinates: only the observer has a position.
Eukleides (Obrecht) makes the syntax resemble geometric notation and avoids Cartesian coordinates; values are typed (point, vector, line, circle, conic); interactive variables are bounded. astra/1 is typed with units (an angle is not a length, a rate is an angle per time) and coordinate-free.
GeoGebra, JSXGraph’s JessieCode, CindyScript drive a dependency graph from sliders and treat labels as handles on objects. In astra/1 the driving variable is the model’s kinematic variable; every object has an ASCII identifier that is also its reference address, and a display symbol for the figure.
Dennis Duke’s animations of the Almagest models compute every position in closed form from one time variable with named rates and lengths, and show the equivalence of two models by a slider between them. In astra/1 that slider is the fade between the members of a superposition; what Duke shows, a derivation states with its hypotheses.
Brandon Rhodes’ SVGs keep parameter fitting apart from drawing and state their scale conventions. In astra/1 values stand in parametrisations with a source or an explicit gap each, and a figure text states orientation, framing and drawing values.

None of these was taken over: astra/1 is a language for historical astronomical models, so an observer, a body, a kinematic variable, a source for every number and a rule for every step are part of what makes a text complete.

title: Design notes
text:
The universal frame
What all historical models share, and what the checks test for: one observer; bodies carried by constructed points; kinematic variables; a construction from circles and lines (and the ellipse); observables that are directions from the observer. Ptolemy’s eccentric and epicycle, the equant (seen_from), the Maragha couples, the Copernican transposition to a heliocentric frame, Tycho’s arrangement and Kepler’s ellipse (true_anomaly, ellipse) are expressible. What differs between two of them is visible in the diff of their models; what they share in spite of it is the conclusion of a derivation in their superposition.

title: Design notes
text:
For an AI reader
The texts are small, typed and separate, so a language model can read them as reliably as code: every name resolves, a model has no accidental numbers in it, every number has a page and an owner, every step of an argument names its rule and carries its status, and the sheets restate all of it as tables. An explanation of the difference between two models would quote the diff of their geometries and the derivation of what they share, not a recollection.

title: Design notes
text:
Decisions

Model, parametrisation, state are three things (10 Nov 2026, owner). A model has no values. Values are a text of their own, with an owner and sources. A state is an argument. Different things are true of each.
Three roles. attributed (whose model), witness (the text analysed), author (who wrote the astra text). An exposition is not an authorship.
A diagram of two models is a superposition. Equivalence is a relation derived under hypotheses, never drawn in.
Derivation is an operation after construction. Givens, auxiliary constructions, steps with premises and rules, a conclusion; four checks. The rules are a table with Heath’s wording and pages.
Coordinate-free. The observer is the origin; everything else is relational.
Gaps are explicit. A value without a source needs gap "…"; a partial parametrisation is reported as partial; a step whose rule does not match is “true, not justified”. No check passes by default.
Two evaluators, one op-set, shared vectors. Python for stills and checks, JS for animation.
Drawn as printed, marked as drawn. Drawing values stand in the figure text and never in a parametrisation.
Tokens, not colours. The famulus palette comes from famulus-visualization’s token source.
Reference objects. Every text and every part of it, down to a step of a derivation, has an address.

title: Design notes
text:
Open

A derivation covers its degenerate states only when it argues them separately, by cases. The checks report uncovered states and whether the cases cover every configuration; they do not propose the distinction.
Hypotheses have to fix a parameter; inequalities and incidence hypotheses are not supported.
“Read off the construction” and “calculation” are tested numerically, not replayed symbolically.
Tabulated motions; latitude (the frame is planar); models beyond the solar model wait for their source pages on this machine.

title: Model, parametrisation, state
text:
The model has no values
# Ptolemy's solar model in its eccentric form: the pure geometry.
# The description follows the use Swerdlow makes of the model in The Renaissance of Astronomy (2026), pp. 19–22
# (scan pages 49–52): the earth O, the centre E of the eccentric at the distance e in the direction of the
# apogee, the sun S moving uniformly about E. No value stands here; values are parametrisations.
model solar-eccentric "Ptolemy's solar model, eccentric form"
attributed "Ptolemy"
witness fr:kepler-sec/Swerdlow2026/0049/p04 "the construction, p. 19"
witness fr:kepler-sec/Swerdlow2026/0050/p03 "longitudes, anomalies and the equation, p. 20"
witness fr:kepler-sec/Swerdlow2026/0051/fig02 "Fig. 1.4"
author "Gerd Graßhoff"
tradition ptolemaic
frame geocentric

param R       : length "radius of the eccentric"                in (1, 1000)
param e       : length "eccentricity, the distance OE"          in (0, R / 2)
param lamA    : angle  "longitude of the apogee"
param T       : time   "tropical year"                          in (300, 400)
param kappa_0 : angle  "mean anomaly at t = 0"
display lamA "λ_A"
display kappa_0 "κ̄_0"

variable kappa_bar : angle "mean anomaly about E, counted from the apogee"
law kappa_bar = uniform(period: T, epoch: kappa_0) "the sun moves uniformly about E"
display kappa_bar "κ̄"

O   = observer                        "earth"
E   = O + polar(e, lamA)              "centre of the eccentric"
ecc = circle(E, R)                    "the eccentric"
A   = E + polar(R, lamA)              "apogee"
B   = E - polar(R, lamA)              "perigee"
S   = E + polar(R, lamA + kappa_bar)  "sun"
body sun at S

observe lam_bar = direction(E, S)     "mean longitude"
observe lam     = direction(O, S)     "true longitude"
observe kappa   = lam - lamA          "true anomaly about O"
observe c       = lam_bar - lam       "equation of centre, mean minus true longitude"
display lam_bar "λ̄_S"
display lam "λ_S"
display kappa "κ"

# stated propositions: checked over the parameter space and all states, not derived here
proposition p1: equal(lam_bar, lamA + kappa_bar) "the mean longitude is the longitude of the apogee plus the mean anomaly"
proposition p2: equal(kappa, kappa_bar - c)      "the true anomaly is the mean anomaly less the equation"
proposition p5: equal(lam, lam_bar - c)           "the true longitude is the mean longitude less the equation"
proposition p3: collinear(A, E, B)               "the apsidal line passes through E"
proposition p4: collinear(A, O, B)               "and through O"
A model text that writes param R = 60 … or gives a source to a value is refused, with a message that says where the value belongs. Because the model has no values, it is checked where it lives: over its parameter space (48 sampled points, each parameter in its range, ranges that depend on other parameters evaluated inside the sample) and its states (the kinematic variable through a revolution). A proposition stated in a model holds when it holds in every one of these configurations. equal(distance(O, E), R / 24) is true for Ptolemy’s values and is not a property of the model; stated in the model, it fails.

section: The kinematic variable and its law
text:
The kinematic variable and its law
variable kappa_bar : angle declares what varies. law kappa_bar = uniform(period: T, epoch: kappa_0) says how it runs in time, with the period and the epoch as ordinary parameters. A state names the variable directly (kappa_bar = 41°) or a time (t = 100 d), which the law turns into a value of the variable. A variable without a law is free; a figure of a model whose period has no value still moves, through the variable.

title: Model, parametrisation, state
section: Drawing values are not attested values
text:
Drawing values are not attested values
A figure may be drawn with other values than the attested ones: drawn with e = 16. These are marked as drawing values in the figure text, in the figure’s corner and in its sheet, and they never touch the parametrisation. A figure without any parametrisation is drawn with drawing values only — the epicyclic form, to which the pages give no values of its own.

# circle about the earth O; the sun moves on the epicycle "in the opposite direction through κ̄ about C from OC
# extended", so that the radius of the epicycle keeps the direction of the apsidal line.
model solar-epicyclic "Ptolemy's solar model, epicyclic form"
attributed "Ptolemy"
witness fr:kepler-sec/Swerdlow2026/0049/p04 "the construction, p. 19"
witness fr:kepler-sec/Swerdlow2026/0050/fig01 "Fig. 1.2"
author "Gerd Graßhoff"
tradition ptolemaic
frame geocentric

param R'      : length "radius of the deferent, the circle about O"   in (1, 1000)
param r       : length "radius of the epicycle"                       in (0, R' / 2)
param lamA    : angle  "longitude of the apogee"
param T       : time   "tropical year"                                in (300, 400)
param kappa_0 : angle  "mean anomaly at t = 0"
display lamA "λ_A"
display kappa_0 "κ̄_0"

variable kappa_bar : angle "mean anomaly: the motion of C about O, and of the sun about C in the opposite sense"
law kappa_bar = uniform(period: T, epoch: kappa_0) "C moves uniformly about O"
display kappa_bar "κ̄"

O   = observer                        "earth"
def = circle(O, R')                   "the deferent"
A'  = O + polar(R', lamA)             "apogee of the deferent"
B'  = O - polar(R', lamA)             "perigee of the deferent"
C   = O + polar(R', lamA + kappa_bar) "centre of the epicycle"
epi = circle(C, r)                    "the epicycle"
S'  = C + polar(r, lamA)              "sun"
body sun at S'

observe lam = direction(O, S')        "true longitude"
display lam "λ_S"

proposition p1: parallel(line(C, S'), line(O, A')) "the radius of the epicycle stays parallel to the apsidal line"
proposition p2: collinear(A', O, B')               "the apsidal line passes through O"

title: The texts
text:
Gaps

Almagest III 3–4 is not in PDAI on this machine; the attribution to Ptolemy and the loci “3.4; 3.13” are as Swerdlow’s page gives them.
No epoch is given on the pages; kappa_0 = 0° is a stated convention.
Models with an equant, the Maragha couples, the Copernican and Keplerian models are not written: their source pages are not located on this machine.

title: The package and a project’s own texts
text: The texts of this workspace — models, parametrisations, superpositions, figures, derivations, expositions — are offered to other documents as a package. A document does not use “astra” at large. It declares what it imports, and exactly that is available to it.

title: The package and a project’s own texts
text:
The manifest
PACKAGE.yaml is written by famulus-astra package --write and never by hand. It lists every shared text:
schema: famulus-package/1
name: astra
address: fr:astra
notation: astra/1
version: 0.3.0
groups:
  solar:
    texts:
    - id: solar-eccentric-epicyclic
      kind: superposition
      title: Eccentric and epicyclic form of Ptolemy's solar model, superposed
      file: examples/solar/solar-eccentric-epicyclic.astra
      sha256: …
      needs: [solar-eccentric, solar-epicyclic]
A group is a folder under examples/ (solar, kepler, euler). needs are the texts a text names: the model of a parametrisation, the members of a superposition, the context and the values of a figure or a derivation. They are read from the parsed text, not from its wording. The hash is the SHA-256 of the source: an importing document can record against which state of a text it was written.
famulus-astra package --check says where the manifest and the texts differ, and the test suite fails when the manifest is behind. fr:astra names the package, fr:astra/<group> lists a group.

title: The package and a project’s own texts
text:
Importing it into a notebook
A Famulus notebook project declares its imports in famulus.yml:
imports:
  solar: fr:astra/solar                 # a group
  equant: fr:astra/kepler-equant        # one text, with the texts it rests on
  # astra: fr:astra@rel:0.3.0           # the whole package, pinned to a version
A text always comes with its closure over needs: importing a figure brings the derivation it draws, the superposition that derivation works in, the two models, and the parametrisations. What the declaration does in the notebook:

a segment {{< famulus fr:astra/<id> animation|svg|argument|exposition >}} shows an imported text; a text outside the imports is a gap that names the declaration which would import it;
the project’s famulus.lock records the hash of every imported text in use; when a text of the package changes, the segments that rest on it are stale until the author has looked and locked again;
cells ask the package through the steps astra:derive, astra:check and astra:positions and receive tables with counted values an oracle can be set against;
an instruction session lays exactly the imported texts before the engine that writes a project’s own text.

The notebook side is described in the Famulus Notebook documentation (project, references).

title: The package and a project’s own texts
text:
A project’s own texts
A project keeps texts of its own in a folder astra/ beside its notebooks. They may be of every kind: a figure of a shared derivation with a line of sight and a narration; a model of its own, superposed with a shared model, with a parametrisation that takes attested values over (use Ecc = solar-eccentric.ptolemy) and a figure. They join the workspace through --root <dir> (or FAMULUS_ASTRA_PATH):
famulus-astra --root ~/work/aequivalenz/astra check solar-mean-sun
famulus-astra --root ~/work/aequivalenz/astra svg solar-fig-mean-sun
A project’s text names shared texts by id. A shared text never names a project’s text, a project’s text never enters the manifest, and an id used on both sides is an error of that id. Every rule of the language holds for a project’s text as for a shared one: a model holds no values and needs its witness; a value needs its source or a stated gap.

title: The package and a project’s own texts
text:
Positions
famulus-astra positions solar-fig-1-2 Ecc.S "Epi.S'" --steps 6
lists where the named points of a figure stand at equally spaced states of one revolution — by default the bodies — and, for two points, their distance and its maximum. A model, a superposition or a derivation has no values; it is evaluated under a parametrisation named with --with. The table states what was computed with which values. It proves nothing: that two points coincide for every admissible value is what a derivation shows.

title: Reference objects
text:
Every astra text and each of its parts is a Famulus reference object (famulus-ref/2, namespace astra; vocabulary 2.4.0).
Former names resolve: fr:astra/solar-equivalence, solar-proportional, solar-eccentric-epicyclic-proportional and solar-complete answer with the object they now are and say alias_of.

title: Reference objects
text:
Resolution

famulus-astra fr fr:astra/solar-equivalence-equal-radii/d6 answers from the workspace and build/<id>/ (building first if the text is newer than its build).
The famulus-reference resolver on :5135 (/api/describe?ref=fr:astra/…, MCP fr_describe) delegates astra addresses to famulus_astronomica.fr.describe when the package is installed on the node, and otherwise answers with an explicit gap.

$ curl "$FAMULUS_REFERENCE/api/describe?ref=fr:astra/solar-equivalence-equal-radii/d6"   # the reference service of the node
{"ref":"fr:astra/solar-equivalence-equal-radii/d6","kind":"astra_step","found":true,
 "proposition":"parallel(line(O, Ecc.E), line(Epi.C, Ecc.S))","from":["d2","d5"],"by":"Elements I.33",
 "status":"justified","binding":{"A":"O","B":"Epi.C","C":"Ecc.E","D":"Ecc.S"},
 "degenerate_at":["kappa_bar = 0°","kappa_bar = 180°"], …}

title: Reference objects
text:
Writing about a model
Because every part has an address, prose can say exactly what it speaks of: “by fr:astra/solar-equivalence-equal-radii/d6, OE is parallel to CS; the step is an instance of Elements I.33 and fails to apply at the apsides”. The sheet is the table such a passage refers to; the figure shows the step.

title: Reference objects
text:
What changed in famulus-reference (10 Nov 2026)
spec/kinds.yaml 2.4.0: fr:astra/<text>[/<object>]; the grammar-level kind of a text is astra_text, the resolver names the kind (astra_model, astra_parametrisation, astra_superposition, astra_figure, astra_derivation) and of an object (astra_parameter, astra_variable, astra_object, astra_observable, astra_proposition, astra_value, astra_given, astra_step, astra_computation). Object names may be dotted (Ecc.S, arcs.e). ids.py and the TypeScript twin fr.ts follow; three test vectors were added; both suites pass. title: The animation runtime
text: astra-runtime.js is a dependency-free ES module that animates a figure in the browser. It does not parse astra/1; it reads the figure bundle — the context’s ops, the figure’s parameter values, the scene, the projection and how the figure moves — computes configurations with the same semantics as the Python evaluator, and redraws the figure’s body. The still SVG that the page already contains is the depicted state, so the figure is right before any script runs.

title: The animation runtime
text:
Controller







call
effect




ctl.seek(u)
the state a fraction u of a revolution after the depicted one


ctl.play() / ctl.pause() / ctl.toggle()
run the kinematic variable at speed seconds per revolution (default 24 s)


ctl.set(name, value)
change a parameter value in the drawing (a slider on the eccentricity)


ctl.morph(v)
superpositions: 0 the first member, 0.5 both, 1 the second


ctl.step(name)
figures of derivations: show what a step speaks of


ctl.state()
{ u, state, speed, playing, params, morph, members, step }


ctl.onChange(fn)
called after every frame with the state



The transport has one row per thing to do: play and the state slider with a readout of the variable (and of the time, when the period has a value); for a superposition a slider that fades between the two members; for a figure of a derivation two buttons that go through the steps, with the step’s proposition, rule and status.

title: The animation runtime
text:
Conventions the runtime honours

?t=<seconds> renders the still at that scene time and never starts the loop; ?static holds the depicted state; prefers-reduced-motion: reduce does the same. ?theme=light|dark sets the theme; ?morph=0..1 and ?step=<name> preset the fade and the step.
After every frame the SVG carries data-state and data-ink, an estimate of the inked share of the canvas; a construction that fails in some state sets data-render-error on <html>, as do script errors. These are the conventions of famulus-viz render_check: it photographs an animation at 0.6, 3 and 7 scene seconds and requires the frames to differ and to ink at least 0.2 % of the canvas.
The loop is elapsed-time based (a hidden tab pauses it), so playback speed is independent of frame rate.

title: The animation runtime
text:
Two evaluators, one truth
The Python evaluator renders stills and checks propositions; the JS runtime animates. Both implement spec/ops.yaml. spec/ops-vectors.json holds hand-written cases per op, spec/model-vectors.json every context under sampled and attested values in several states, given by the variable and by a time; node tests/js/run_vectors.mjs replays both against the runtime and pytest runs it (a missing node is a failure, not a skip). The placement rules of the figure are stated once (svg/scene.py) and implemented in both renderers line for line.

title: The animation runtime
text:
Embedding
The docs gallery (docs/gallery/*.html) references ../astra-runtime/astra-runtime.js and the tokens CSS; famulus-astra animate (default) inlines runtime, CSS and bundle into one file that can be served from anywhere or opened from disk. Headless renders use the standalone form.
